# Searching only the files you care about

A file type is a name for a list of file name patterns. `md` is the name for
`*.md`, `*.markdown`, `*.mdx` and a few more. `csv` is the name for `*.csv`.
`readme` is the name for `README*` and `*README`. Once a group of files has a
name, you can pull it into a search, or push it out, with one short flag.

ripgrep ships with a long list of these. You can add your own.

## See what's there: `--type-list`

```
$ rg --type-list
```

You get one type per line: the name, a colon, then its patterns, separated by
commas. It's a long list, so search it with ripgrep itself:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^csv:'
csv: *.csv
```

Some types have two names for the same list. `md` and `markdown` are the same
thing, and so are `py` and `python`. Use whichever you like. Note that the
names work exactly as printed, so `md` is a type and `Markdown` isn't.

## Narrow a search: `--type`, or `-t`

```
$ rg 'annual report' --type md
```

or, more succinctly:

```
$ rg 'annual report' -tmd
```

Repeat the flag to take in more than one type. A file gets searched if it
matches any of them:

```
$ rg 'annual report' -tmd -ttxt -tcsv
```

## Push files out: `--type-not`, or `-T`

```
$ rg 'annual report' --type-not csv
$ rg 'annual report' -Tcsv
```

`-t` means "search files of this type", `-T` means "skip files of this type".
Mix them freely. If a file matches both a `-t` and a `-T`, the flag you wrote
last wins.

Both flags accept the special name `all`. `-tall` searches only the files
ripgrep recognises, and `-Tall` searches only the files it doesn't. Say you
have `my-shell-script` and `my-shell-library.bash` in a folder. Both `-tsh` and
`-tall` search the `.bash` file only, because no `sh` pattern matches the name
`my-shell-script`. `-Tall` searches the other one.

## Define your own: `--type-add`

Give a name, a colon, and a pattern:

```
$ rg --type-add 'notes:*.{md,txt}' -tnotes deadline
```

Repeat the flag to build a type up from several patterns, or to define several
types in one command. You can also build a type out of types you already have,
with `include`:

```
$ rg --type-add 'docs:include:md,txt,readme' -tdocs deadline
```

and then keep adding to it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'docs:include:md,txt,readme' --type-add 'docs:*.rtf' -tdocs deadline
```

Two things to keep straight. `--type-add` only defines the type. It doesn't
filter anything on its own, so you still need the `-t` that uses it. And names
must be letters and numbers only, with no punctuation and no spaces. `all` is
already taken. Get the format wrong and ripgrep tells you:

```
invalid definition (format is type:glob, e.g., html:*.html)
```

Your new type shows up in `rg --type-list` for that command, alongside the
built-in ones. There's also `--type-clear NAME`, which empties a type's pattern
list, in case a built-in one sweeps in files you'd rather it left alone.

## Make a type stick around

Types you add live for exactly one command. Nothing is saved anywhere. To keep
one, either make a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'notes:*.{md,txt}'"
```

or put it in a configuration file. ripgrep reads one when you point the
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable at it:

```
$ cat $HOME/.ripgreprc
# Add my 'notes' type.
--type-add
notes:*.{md,txt}
```

Each line in that file is one argument, handed to ripgrep verbatim, so the
value goes on its own line and takes no quotes.

## Four things worth knowing

**Patterns match the file's name, not the folder it sits in.** A type can say
"every file ending in `.txt`". It can't say "every file under `reports/`". Use
`-g`/`--glob` for anything involving a path.

**Types lose to globs and to ignore files.** `--type` has lower precedence than
`--glob` and lower precedence than the rules in `.gitignore`, `.ignore` and
`.rgignore`. If `-tcsv` finds nothing and you're sure the files are there, an
ignore file is probably hiding them. Add `--no-ignore`, or throw a `-u` or two
at the command to peel the filtering back.

**A type names files. It doesn't teach ripgrep to read them.** `-tpdf` picks
out your PDFs, but ripgrep skips binary files by default, and PDFs are binary.
You'll get no matches from inside them. The same goes for other packed
formats.

**A typo stops the search.** Ask for a type that doesn't exist and you'll see
`unrecognized file type: mardown` rather than a quiet, empty result. Check the
spelling against `rg --type-list`.
